measured-scalar.description: The latest scalar emitted by a repeatable measurement source. Authored lf-num text freezes the value a version states; the source snapshot records whether that measurement ran again.

text-document.description: UTF-8 text from a file or a selected line range.

lf-ask.description: A heading and context for the asks inside it, each answered separately.
lf-ask.x-instructions: Give it a heading that states the shared question or context without leaning on the prose around it, with any eyebrow beside it in an `<hgroup>`. Include the evidence the user needs to answer. Each widget inside that asks for input stays its own ask with its own answer. Wrap the context in a `section` when the document needs a section landmark.
lf-ask.x-example:
What should a full store do?

The beta never reached the cap. This decides what the first workspace at it sees; each option draws its document list once the store fills.

editing: continuesrecommendedDrop the oldest documents Editing continues. My take: this keeps work moving without losing server data. editing: pausedPause offline editing Nothing leaves.

lf-gloss.description: A short explanation the reader can open beside a phrase without leaving its sentence.
lf-gloss.x-instructions: Write a self-contained explanation at the first useful occurrence rather than on every repetition. Keep the phrase out of authored parentheses: print adds the explanation as a parenthetical note.
lf-gloss.x-example: Deploy through a <lf-gloss tip="A thin, end-to-end path through the real system.">walking skeleton</lf-gloss> before parallelizing.

lf-num.description: A measured number in prose, tied to the data run that produced it.
lf-num.x-instructions: Write the value with its unit as the element's text. Bind `source` to the feed that measures it, and set `run` to the receipt `leaf data set` returned. Add `via` when the source id doesn't say which command or query produced it.
lf-num.x-example: The import now takes <lf-num source="import-latency" run="a41f103e236c985b" via="uv run bench-import">184 ms</lf-num> at p95.

lf-text-document.description: A text file from page data, with syntax coloring and an optional Markdown or HTML preview.
lf-text-document.x-instructions: Bind `source` to the page's data source and name the file with `label`. Set `preview` to `markdown` or `html` to add Preview and Source tabs over the same text. `language` colors the source, and defaults to the preview's language. An HTML preview is a separate document that inherits no Leaf styles. With a preview, each tab scrolls inside a box 28rem tall, or `--lf-bound`. To start it collapsed, put it inside `details`.

lf-toc.description: An outline of the document’s h2–h6 headings for navigating its sections and showing the reader’s position.
lf-toc.x-instructions: Write it empty with a stable id. Set `max-level` to leave out deeper headings that are local detail; by default it lists h2 to h6. Give sections or headings ids of your own where a link must keep its target across versions, since the ids Leaf generates aren't stable.
lf-toc.x-example:
Migration plan

Prepare

Take a snapshot.

Check capacity

Leave headroom for the copy.

Move

Shift one cohort at a time.

lf-activity.description: A newest-first feed of the page’s comments, actions, reports, and published revisions.
lf-activity.x-instructions: Write it empty with a stable id.

lf-options.description: Alternatives the user can choose individually or as a set to answer a question.
lf-options.x-instructions: Keep shared premises and evidence with the group (lf-ask can frame its question and context), and each alternative's own case inside its lf-option. For an accept-or-reject proposal, a figure of today beside the change compares both answers, so it stays with the group. Use `multiple` when the picks form one answer because they depend on each other, such as a limit on how many; leave it off for mutually exclusive alternatives. Items the user can answer independently are separate asks (references/authoring-asks.md). The built-in Another option field takes unlisted answers, so add no catch-all option. Use `for` only to point at sections or work items that exist apart from the decision. An option the user adds stays in the group from the log, where the user put it; leave it out of revisions. A `multiple` ask needs the user's Done even when `chosen` is authored. `settled` collapses a decided group while keeping its options and anchors.
lf-options.x-example:
Where should run status appear?

Both choices preserve the existing run detail.

effort: lowrisk: medrecommended Status on the run list One join; failures are visible without a click. effort: nonerisk: low Leave the list alone No work; failures stay one click away.

lf-option.description: One alternative in a decision: a compact label, or a card showing what choosing it gives the user.
lf-option.x-instructions: Start a card with small.tag labels naming the facts that tell the alternatives apart, then a `<strong>` title and a sentence giving its consequence. Mark the option you recommend with `<small class="tag ok">recommended</small>` after its labels, and give the reason in prose. `chosen` records the user's pick. Below, show what choosing it gives the user (references/authoring-asks.md): where options differ in arrangement, structure or mechanism, an svg.drawing thumbnail of each in the same frame, alike except where they differ; where they differ in how an existing interface looks, a capture of each; where they differ in behavior, that behavior working inside each; where they differ in wording, the words as they would appear. Add paragraphs or a fact rail only when that is not enough; a bare label suits an option that needs no case. Direct text takes inline Markdown; block content needs HTML children. A `for` target must stay useful whatever is decided, and does not supply the option's words. Rewriting a picked option needs `restated` ($restated).

lf-code.description: A source-code excerpt with syntax coloring, highlighted lines, and line-anchored remarks.
lf-code.x-instructions: Write the exact code inside pre at column 0, HTML-escaping & before < and >. Set language for source code and omit it for plain transcripts or command output. For excerpts, set lines to the ascending source ranges quoted, such as 1505-1507,1520-1527; hi and lf-note at then use those source numbers. A note addressed to an omitted line captions the elided row.
lf-code.x-example:
def bracket(temp):
    if temp < 0:
        return "steel"
    return "cedar"
Freezing is the only threshold that matters.

lf-note.description: A prose remark anchored to a line or omitted range of its lf-code parent.
lf-note.x-instructions: Set at to the line number as the parent numbers it: 1-based by default, or the source number declared in lines.

lf-chart.description: An Observable Plot chart authored with Plot’s API and sized to its place in the page.
lf-chart.x-instructions: Inside a `<pre>`, write a JavaScript expression for the options object you would pass to `Plot.plot`, HTML-escaping & before < and >. `Plot` and `width` are the names in scope, and the data goes inline. The chart requires an `ariaLabel` describing it. Leave `width` and `height` out of the options: read `width` to fit the ticks to the room, and set a height other than the default with `data-height` on the element. Write dates as ISO strings on an explicitly typed time scale, `utc` for days and months, and give moments a time zone, such as 2026-06-01T14:00Z. Use `var(--series-N)` for constant or categorical colors; a continuous color scale needs a Plot scheme. Title the chart in the heading or prose around it rather than with Plot's `title`. Label on the chart each value the page's argument cites, such as a spike the prose explains, with a text mark beside the point. When `page check --render` reports overlapping labels, use fewer category ticks, choose them by `width`, or give the axis label more margin.
lf-chart.x-example:
{
  ariaLabel: "Hours to first review by week: backend fell from 31 to 12, frontend from 18 to 11",
  x: {type: "utc", ticks: "monday", label: null},
  y: {grid: true, label: "hours to first review"},
  color: {legend: true, range: ["var(--series-1)", "var(--series-2)"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(
      [
        {week: "2026-05-04", team: "backend", hours: 31},
        {week: "2026-05-11", team: "backend", hours: 26},
        {week: "2026-05-18", team: "backend", hours: 12},
        {week: "2026-05-04", team: "frontend", hours: 18},
        {week: "2026-05-11", team: "frontend", hours: 21},
        {week: "2026-05-18", team: "frontend", hours: 11},
      ],
      {x: "week", y: "hours", stroke: "team", marker: true},
    ),
  ],
}

lf-shot.description: A before-and-after pair of screenshots under a draggable divider, with optional outlines of what changed and a view of the changed pixels.
lf-shot.x-instructions: Use it for two versions of an interface. Set `before` and `after` to the paths `leaf page media` prints, and describe the pair in `alt`. `authoring-evidence.md`, "Source files and media", covers making captures and when to add `outlines` or `pixels`. Put explanation in the prose around the pair, not inside the element. When a decision turns on the change, put the pair inside the option that proposes it, or, for an accept-or-reject ask, with the group, where it shows both answers.
lf-shot.x-example:
The option cards

The chips now sit above the title, so a scanning eye reads cost before prose.

lf-board.description: Cards grouped into columns for scanning work and status, with movement and reordering available.
lf-board.x-instructions: Use a board to show grouped work and status. When the user must make changes or decisions, give them explicit controls or `lf-options` rather than relying on moving cards. When revising, keep each card the user moved in the column they chose, unless the revision retracts that move by marking the card, not the board, `restated` (`authoring-revisions.md`, "Honor user state").
lf-board.x-example: Heated perch Wire the south feeder. Squirrel baffle Camera mount

lf-column.description: One named board column, including empty columns the user can move a card into.
lf-column.x-instructions: Write a label that names the column on its own. Use tone when landing here carries a status judgment, such as blocked, needing review, or done; otherwise leave it neutral.

lf-card.description: One board card whose identity and comments survive user moves.
lf-card.x-instructions: Lead with a `<strong>` title and follow with prose. Keep its id stable across moves. Rewriting a card the user moved needs restated; read $restated.

lf-tabs.description: Several views shown one at a time: page navigation, a tabbed box, or a queue beside its open item.
lf-tabs.x-instructions: The first `lf-tabs` written directly in `main` is the page's navigation; any other tab set is a framed box within the page. Put the page's title and lede before page tabs, and the main current view first. Make each `lf-tab` a self-contained view; history, threads, versions and sign-off belong to the whole page. When current work no longer needs a view, remove it, keeping any context still needed, and any passage that anchors an open thread or a standing decision, in a `details` inside the relevant tab. Use `list="side"` for a queue listed beside the item it opens.
lf-tabs.x-example:
Wire the first site this week.

Keep the original outcome and constraints in reach.

lf-tally.description: A count of the open asks in one region, such as the decisions left in a queue, with an optional control that goes to the next one.
lf-tally.x-instructions: Write it empty with a stable id, and set `for` to the region whose asks it counts, such as a side-list `lf-tabs` queue. Place it where the reader looks for the queue's state, such as a workspace header beside its `.tag` chips. Add `next` for a Next on me control that steps through the asks waiting on the user. Don't also state the count in prose or chips; the tally keeps it current.
lf-tally.x-prepaint: 00 of 00 to answerNothing to answer

Release triage

Ship it Hold for a canary

Remove the flag?

Remove it Keep it a release

lf-tab.description: One labeled view in a tab set, optionally summarized and grouped in a side-list queue.
lf-tab.x-instructions: In a side-list queue each item's `summary` shows under its label, so the user can choose an item without opening it. Start the summary with what the item is about, such as the problem a ticket reports, unless the label already says so, then what sets it apart from its neighbours, such as its age or suggested outcome. Leave out the item's group, which its heading shows. Where items fall into kinds the user works through in turn, such as merge, close and FYI, give each item its kind as `group` and place each kind's items together in the order to take them; adjacent tabs with the same group share one heading. Keep ids distinct across tabs, which share the page's id space.

lf-draft.description: A block of text the user owns and can rewrite in place, with recorded revision history.
lf-draft.x-instructions:
Write the exact Markdown source as `
`, one newline, the HTML-escaped source (& before < and >), then `
` right after it. HTML drops that first newline; every later character, indentation and trailing newlines included, is part of the draft. For a change you propose to existing prose, use a suggestion instead. With `needed`, a draft asks the user for an edit; without it, it is an optional editing surface. Use lf-ask when the request needs its own heading and evidence, or page sign-off to approve the whole page. Keep the user's exact source on revision (authoring-revisions.md, "Honor user state"); to replace an edited passage on purpose, write the new text and mark the draft `restated` ($restated).
lf-draft.x-example: Adds --dry-run to every mutating command.

lf-sample.description: A quotation of page content, either static or an operable child Leaf page.
lf-sample.x-instructions: For a live child page, put its main content in one direct template[data-sample] with a stable id. Use window for a whole Leaf window including its chrome; chrome="floating" or chrome="classic" shows it in that chrome rather than the reader's own. Keep invented content visibly fictional. Read live-samples.md for child-page interaction, reset, and isolation.

chrome.description: For a window sample, the chrome its child page reads with; without it, the reader's own preference.

lf-sample.x-example: effort: lowPaper maps Nothing to charge. effort: medrecommendedDedicated GPS Offline maps, week-long battery. My take: this is the better field tool.

lf-pane.description: A reading region with an optional header and footer, independently scrollable inside a full-height workspace.
lf-pane.x-instructions: For independent scrolling, place the pane as a full-height workspace’s body or a direct cell; elsewhere the page scrolls. Wrap multiple body blocks in one div or section. Use label to name the region accessibly and its header for the visible heading. Put action widgets in the direct footer when they should remain reachable as the body scrolls.
lf-pane.x-example: Read the selected record.
